02 Antipsychotics · class card

Anticholinergic

anticholinergics for antipsychotic movement effects · benztropine · diphenhydramine · trihexyphenidyl

Key point
  • Benztropine, trihexyphenidyl and diphenhydramine block muscarinic receptors the striatal acetylcholine-dopamine balance returns acute dystonia and parkinsonism ease
  • No benefit in tardive dyskinesia, which they may worsen; for akathisia, propranolol is preferred
  • Class adverse effects: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, big pupils and delirium, worst in older adults; a large dose or a second anticholinergic anticholinergic toxicity
Drugs

Benztropine: acts mainly in the brain on muscarinic receptors; injected for acute dystonia, then taken by mouth

Trihexyphenidyl: the same central muscarinic block; antipsychotic movement effects and Parkinson tremor

Diphenhydramine Benadryl: first-generation antihistamine with strong antimuscarinic action; sedating; given by injection for dystonia

Mechanism

Antipsychotic dopamine blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway striatal acetylcholine outweighs dopamine dystonia and parkinsonism

in the brain balance restored dystonia eases within minutes Benztropine mechanism of benefitMuscarinic block: the only action established as therapeutic in parkinsonismAntihistamine action: present, with no established therapeutic role in parkinsonism

Muscarinic block outside the brain less secretion from sweat and salivary glands, less contraction of bladder and bowel the adverse effects

Uses

Acute dystonia: benztropine or diphenhydramine by injection; typically in 3 to 5 minutes Onset of IV reliefIn practice: no real difference in onset between IV and intramuscular injectionImprovement after injection: sometimes within a few minutes

Prevention: with an intramuscular first-generation antipsychotic in a high-risk patient (young man, earlier extrapyramidal effects)

Drug-induced parkinsonism: short-term relief only, when the antipsychotic dose cannot come down

Parkinson disease: tremor and rigidity improve, slowness does not

Akathisia: a lesser option; propranolol is preferred

Not for tardive dyskinesia Other uses of diphenhydramineMay serve as an over-the-counter sleep aidMay be used for motion sickness

Adverse effects

Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention (worst with an enlarged prostate), big pupils, fast pulse

Less sweating heat intolerance and hyperthermia

and delirium, most in older adults; can worsen psychosis Benztropine toxic psychosisConfusion, disorientation, memory lossVisual hallucinationsEarlier psychotic symptoms: worsening

Angle-closure glaucoma from pupil dilation

Diphenhydramine: sedation; a false-positive phencyclidine urine screen

Nightly diphenhydramine for sleep: constipation with hard, infrequent stools for two months, good diet, normal exam

Constipation on diphenhydramine, a reversible drug cause: choose stopping the diphenhydramine

Common wrong answers: anorectal manometry, colon transit study, fiber, abdominal X-ray

Constipation with a reversible drug cause: further tests unnecessary until a trial off the drug

Anticholinergic toxicityHot, dry, flushed skin, big pupils, fast pulse and delirium, muscle tone normal; from a large dose or stacked anticholinergics

If the toxicity is severe and no tricyclic is involved, choose physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor.

Anticholinergic delirium: agitated and confused for a day on haloperidol plus benztropine

Findings of anticholinergic delirium: fever, fast pulse, high blood pressure, dry red skin, wide pupils

Mimics of anticholinergic delirium: amphetamine psychosis, hallucinogen delirium, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, depression, schizophrenia

Dry skin with normal tone: anticholinergic delirium

Rigidity: points to neuroleptic malignant syndrome

Sweating: points to a stimulant

Tardive dyskinesiaAnticholinergics bring no relief, and in some patients the movements grow worse

If tardive dyskinesia appears in a patient taking benztropine, choose stopping the benztropine.

An older adultCognitive and anticholinergic effects raise the risk of delirium; urinary retention with an enlarged prostate

If an older adult develops parkinsonism on an antipsychotic, choose a lower antipsychotic dose or amantadine over an anticholinergic.

Drug interactions
DrugEffectManagement
Another anticholinergic: a low-potency or phenothiazine antipsychotic, clozapine, a tricyclic, diphenhydramineAdditive block; heat stroke and paralytic ileus, sometimes fatal, have been reported Report fever, heat intolerance or bowel symptoms promptly
Alcohol, sedatives or tranquilizers, with diphenhydramineDrowsiness may increaseAvoid alcohol; ask before adding a sedative

Practice
  1. 19-year-old man given intramuscular haloperidol for agitation 3 hours later his neck twists to one side and his eyes roll upward alert and oriented; temperature normal intravenous benztropine; the spasm eases within minutes → Muscarinic receptor blockade → with dopamine blocked, acetylcholine outweighs it in the striatum; blocking muscarinic receptors restores the balance and ends the spasm
  2. 74-year-old man with schizophrenia and an enlarged prostate takes haloperidol; a second drug was added 2 weeks ago for stiffness and a tremor now strains to urinate and passes hard stools; dry mouth bladder scan: large volume after voiding → Benztropine → its muscarinic block causes urinary retention, most of all with prostatic enlargement, along with constipation and a dry mouth; levodopa is not used for antipsychotic parkinsonism, and propranolol blocks beta receptors
  3. 63-year-old woman with Parkinson disease on carbidopa-levodopa a resting pill-rolling tremor of the right hand and cogwheel rigidity still bother her she also moves slowly, with a shuffling gait and small handwriting her neurologist adds trihexyphenidyl → Bradykinesia → trihexyphenidyl and benztropine ease the tremor and rigidity of Parkinson disease, which reflect relative cholinergic excess, but leave slowness of movement unchanged
